title: Hepatitis A, Hepatitis C and Wilson Disease: Markers That Mislead
summary: Learn why total anti-HAV cannot confirm acute hepatitis A, why a modest or normal ALT does not mean mild hepatitis C, and why a normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 22 Hit 13 (Wilson disease), Hit 17 (IgM anti-HAV, acute hepatitis A), Trap 4 (modest ALT in HCV) and Trap 5 (normal ceruloplasmin). Checked against ACIP 2020 (Nelson), CDC 2020 HCV screening (Schillie), Chen and Morgan 2006, Uto 2012, the AASLD 2023 Wilson summary (Alkhouri), Schroeder 2021, Penning 2023 and Seo 2012. The reviewer’s figures that ceruloplasmin is normal in up to 15% of Wilson patients (35% with hepatic disease) were not found in the open sources read and are not taught (pending). Open sources add context the reviewer omits: relapsing hepatitis A (10–15% of symptomatic cases, up to 6 months), and Kayser-Fleischer rings absent in about 60% of hepatic presentations. Not taught: Wilson treatment, hepatitis A vaccination schedules, HCV treatment, Hit 14 (hepatitis etiology percentages).

objectives: Distinguish IgM anti-HAV from IgG and total anti-HAV and interpret a total-positive, IgM-negative result.
Explain why a modest or normal ALT does not indicate a mild course of hepatitis C.
Explain the mechanism of low ceruloplasmin in Wilson disease and list the tests needed when ceruloplasmin is normal.

scenes.title: Three livers, three reassuring numbers
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Three patients: (1) a 28-year-old with jaundice after travel, ALT very high, total anti-HAV positive; (2) a 45-year-old blood donor, anti-HCV reactive and HCV RNA detected, ALT within the reference interval; (3) a 19-year-old with unexplained hepatitis and a hand tremor, serum ceruloplasmin 24 mg/dL (within the reference interval). Question token: “Which number is fooling us?”

cues.text: Three patients. A traveller with jaundice and a positive total hepatitis A antibody. A blood donor with hepatitis C RNA but a normal ALT.
And a nineteen-year-old with unexplained hepatitis, a tremor, and a normal ceruloplasmin.
Each has one reassuring-looking number. Which ones are fooling us?

scenes.title: Hepatitis A: IgM says now, IgG says ever
scenes.altText: Schematic timeline of hepatitis A (ACIP 2020). Spread by the fecal-oral route; average incubation 28 days (range 15–50). Self-limited; does not cause chronic infection, although 10–15% of symptomatic people have prolonged or relapsing illness lasting up to 6 months. IgM anti-HAV becomes detectable within 5–10 days of symptom onset in most people, peaks within 1 month and is usually undetectable within 6 months. IgG anti-HAV appears early, lasts for life and protects; vaccination also produces IgG. Total anti-HAV measures IgG plus IgM: total positive with IgM negative = immune (past infection or vaccination). Acute infection is confirmed by IgM anti-HAV or HAV RNA; test IgM only in symptomatic people suspected of hepatitis A, to limit false positives.

cues.text: Hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route, with an average incubation of about four weeks. It is self-limited and does not become chronic, though some symptomatic patients relapse for up to six months.
IgM anti-HAV marks acute infection. It appears within about five to ten days of symptoms, peaks within a month, and usually disappears by six months.
IgG anti-HAV appears early and stays for life, after infection or after vaccination. A total antibody test counts IgG and IgM together, so a positive total alone cannot tell now from ever.
Total positive with IgM negative means immune. To limit false positives, IgM is tested only in symptomatic people suspected of hepatitis A.

props.label: IgM anti-HAV: days 5–10 → gone by ~6 mo

scenes.title: Hepatitis C: quiet enzymes, persistent virus
scenes.altText: Hepatitis C natural history card. Acute infection is usually asymptomatic or mild; jaundice in 20–30% (CDC 2020). About 75–85% of infected people progress to chronic infection (Chen and Morgan 2006); CDC 2020 states “more than half”. About 5–25% with chronic hepatitis C develop cirrhosis over 10–20 years; with cirrhosis, HCC risk is 1–4% per year (CDC 2020). ALT card (Uto 2012 review): ALT is within the reference interval in about 30% of HCV carriers and below twice the upper limit in about 40%; many such carriers have mild disease, but fibrosis stage 2 or worse was found in 22% of biopsied normal-ALT cases in one report, and ALT can rise later. Conclusion: a modest ALT does not guarantee mild disease.

cues.text: Hepatitis C is quiet from the start. Acute infection is usually silent or mild, and only about a fifth to a third of people become jaundiced.
Yet most infections persist: about seventy-five to eighty-five percent become chronic in a widely cited review, and the CDC says more than half.
Chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis in about five to twenty-five percent over ten to twenty years, and cirrhosis carries a yearly liver cancer risk of one to four percent.
The enzymes stay quiet too. ALT is normal in about thirty percent of carriers, and fibrosis can be present despite a normal ALT. A modest ALT does not guarantee mild disease.

scenes.title: Wilson disease: one normal ceruloplasmin is not enough
scenes.altText: Mechanism card (AASLD 2023 summary): Wilson disease needs two disease-causing variants in ATP7B on chromosome 13, a hepatocyte copper-transporting ATPase that excretes copper into bile and loads copper onto ceruloplasmin; copper-free apoceruloplasmin is cleared faster, so serum ceruloplasmin is typically low (often below 14 mg/dL; normal above 20). Caveat card: normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease; it can be falsely raised during an acute inflammatory response, and low values also occur without Wilson disease (other cirrhosis, fatty liver, about 20% of heterozygous carriers). Work-up card: basal 24-hour urinary copper above 100 µg in symptomatic patients; hepatic copper above 250 µg/g; slit-lamp for Kayser-Fleischer rings (about 90% with neurological disease, absent in about 60% with hepatic disease); ATP7B genetic testing; Leipzig score. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Wilson disease needs two faulty copies of ATP7B, on chromosome thirteen. The pump normally sends copper into bile and loads it onto ceruloplasmin; without it, ceruloplasmin is usually low.
But a normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease. It can rise during acute inflammation, and low values also occur in other liver disease and in some carriers.

So look further: a twenty-four-hour urine copper above one hundred micrograms, liver copper above two hundred fifty micrograms per gram, a slit-lamp search for Kayser-Fleischer rings, and ATP7B testing.
Back to the hook. The traveller needs IgM anti-HAV. The donor has chronic hepatitis C despite a normal ALT. And the nineteen-year-old still needs copper studies.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Modest or normal ALT means mild hepatitis C” (✓ most infections become chronic and fibrosis can be present with normal ALT); “Normal ceruloplasmin rules out Wilson disease” (✓ check 24-hour urinary copper, hepatic copper, Kayser-Fleischer rings, ATP7B); “Positive total anti-HAV means acute hepatitis A” (✓ total includes lifelong IgG; acute needs IgM anti-HAV or HAV RNA).

cues.text: Trap one: a modest ALT means mild hepatitis C. No: most infections become chronic, and fibrosis can hide behind a normal ALT.
Trap two: a normal ceruloplasmin rules out Wilson disease. No: check urine copper, liver copper, Kayser-Fleischer rings and the gene.
Trap three: a positive total hepatitis A antibody means acute infection. No: total includes lifelong IgG. Acute needs IgM anti-HAV or viral RNA.

scenes.title: A leaves, C stays, copper hides
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “A leaves, C stays, copper hides.” Hepatitis A is a guest that leaves and never becomes chronic (IgM is the visit, IgG the lifelong souvenir); hepatitis C quietly stays (normal ALT does not mean it left); Wilson copper hides behind a normal ceruloplasmin (look in urine, liver and eyes). Tokens for each. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: A leaves, C stays, copper hides. Hepatitis A leaves and never becomes chronic, with IgM for the visit and IgG as a lifelong souvenir. Hepatitis C quietly stays. Wilson copper hides behind a normal ceruloplasmin.

Where it breaks: hepatitis A can relapse for up to six months, and rarely causes liver failure; some people clear hepatitis C on their own, and treatment cures most of the rest; and a low ceruloplasmin does not prove Wilson disease.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Acute hepatitis A = IgM anti-HAV · total anti-HAV alone may be lifelong IgG”, “Normal ALT does not mean mild hepatitis C · normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease”.

cues.text: Confirm acute hepatitis A with IgM rather than total antibody, never call hepatitis C mild because the ALT is modest, and never exclude Wilson disease on a normal ceruloplasmin alone.

props.label: Acute hepatitis A = IgM anti-HAV · total alone may be lifelong IgG
Normal ALT ≠ mild HCV · normal ceruloplasmin ≠ no Wilson

explanation.what: Plain language: three liver conditions where one comforting number can mislead. In hepatitis A, a positive “total” antibody may only show old immunity. In hepatitis C, the liver enzyme ALT can stay normal while the virus persists. In Wilson disease, the copper-carrying protein ceruloplasmin can look normal even though copper is building up. Scientific terms: IgM anti-HAV, IgG anti-HAV, total anti-HAV, HAV RNA, relapsing hepatitis A, chronic HCV infection, persistently normal ALT, fibrosis, ATP7B, apoceruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, hepatic copper, Kayser-Fleischer rings, Leipzig score.
explanation.why: Hepatitis A IgG lasts for life, so a total antibody test that includes IgG stays positive after any past infection or vaccination. ALT reflects hepatocyte injury, and HCV can persist while ALT stays normal, so ALT does not reliably track viral persistence or fibrosis. ATP7B loss impairs copper loading onto ceruloplasmin, and copper-free apoceruloplasmin is cleared faster, so levels are usually low, but ceruloplasmin also rises with inflammation and falls in other liver disease, which makes it neither sensitive nor specific enough on its own.
explanation.measure: Hepatitis A: IgM anti-HAV detectable within 5–10 days of symptoms, peaks within 1 month, usually undetectable within 6 months; acute infection confirmed by IgM anti-HAV or HAV RNA; total positive with IgM negative = immune. Hepatitis C: about 75–85% become chronic (CDC: more than half); ALT normal in about 30% of carriers. Wilson disease: ceruloplasmin typically below 14 mg/dL (normal above 20); basal 24-hour urinary copper above 100 µg in symptomatic patients; hepatic copper above 250 µg/g; slit-lamp for Kayser-Fleischer rings; ATP7B testing.
explanation.differs: IgM anti-HAV (acute) vs IgG anti-HAV (past infection or vaccine, lifelong); HCV viral persistence vs ALT activity; low ceruloplasmin in Wilson disease vs low ceruloplasmin in other cirrhosis, fatty liver or heterozygous carriers.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: interpret total anti-HAV positive with IgM negative, reject “normal ALT means mild hepatitis C”, and choose 24-hour urinary copper or slit-lamp examination when ceruloplasmin is normal in suspected Wilson disease.

comparisons.title: IgM vs IgG anti-HAV
comparisons.distinguisher: Total anti-HAV measures both, so only IgM (or HAV RNA) shows acute infection.

comparisons.title: Hepatitis A vs hepatitis C outcome
comparisons.distinguisher: Hepatitis A never becomes chronic; hepatitis C usually persists, whatever the ALT.

mnemonic.text: A leaves, C stays, copper hides.
mnemonic.explanation: Hepatitis A never becomes chronic (IgM for the visit, IgG as a lifelong souvenir); hepatitis C quietly persists despite a quiet ALT; Wilson copper can hide behind a normal ceruloplasmin.
mnemonic.limitation: Hepatitis A can relapse for up to 6 months and rarely (under 1%) causes fulminant liver failure; some people clear hepatitis C spontaneously and treatment cures most others; a low ceruloplasmin does not prove Wilson disease.

analogyLimitations: Percentages come from the cited reviews and guidance; cohorts and definitions of normal ALT differ.
takeaway: Confirm acute hepatitis A with IgM rather than total antibody, never call hepatitis C mild because the ALT is modest, and never exclude Wilson disease on a normal ceruloplasmin alone.

questions.stem: A symptomatic adult has a positive total anti-HAV and a negative IgM anti-HAV. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Immune to hepatitis A from past infection or vaccination; not acute hepatitis A
options.rationale: Correct. Total anti-HAV includes lifelong IgG; with IgM negative, the person is considered immune, so another cause of the illness should be sought.
Incorrect. Acute infection is shown by IgM anti-HAV or HAV RNA, and IgM is negative.
Incorrect. Hepatitis A does not cause chronic infection.

options.text: A false-positive total antibody that should be ignored
options.rationale: Incorrect. Total positive with IgM negative is the expected pattern of immunity, not an error.

questions.stem: A blood donor has detectable HCV RNA on two occasions six months apart, and every ALT result is within the reference interval. Which statement is correct?

options.text: This is chronic HCV infection; a normal ALT does not exclude significant fibrosis
options.rationale: Correct. ALT is normal in about 30% of HCV carriers, and fibrosis stage 2 or worse has been found in some with normal ALT.

options.text: A normal ALT means the infection has cleared
options.rationale: Incorrect. Persistent HCV RNA shows ongoing infection; clearance means RNA becomes undetectable.

options.text: A normal ALT means the disease cannot progress
options.rationale: Incorrect. ALT can rise later, and fibrosis may already be present.

options.text: Chronic hepatitis C requires ALT above 10 times the upper limit
options.rationale: Incorrect. ALT above 10 times the upper limit is often seen in acute infection; chronic infection is defined by HCV RNA persisting for at least 6 months, not by ALT level.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with unexplained hepatitis and a tremor has a serum ceruloplasmin of 24 mg/dL. What is the best next laboratory step for possible Wilson disease?

options.text: Basal 24-hour urinary copper, with slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings
options.rationale: Correct. A normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude Wilson disease; urinary copper above 100 µg/24 h in a symptomatic patient supports it.

options.text: Exclude Wilson disease because ceruloplasmin is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Normal ceruloplasmin values do not exclude Wilson disease, and inflammation can raise ceruloplasmin.

options.text: Repeat ceruloplasmin only; no other test is useful
options.rationale: Incorrect. Relying on ceruloplasmin alone is not sufficient for diagnosis.

options.text: Measure serum ferritin and transferrin saturation to diagnose Wilson disease
options.rationale: Incorrect. These are iron studies; Wilson disease is evaluated with copper studies, rings and ATP7B testing.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer’s figures that ceruloplasmin is normal in up to 15% of Wilson patients (35% with hepatic disease) were not found in the open sources read. The AASLD 2023 summary states qualitatively that normal values do not exclude and low values do not confirm Wilson disease, that ceruloplasmin can be low or elevated in acute liver failure, and that Kayser-Fleischer rings are absent in about 60% of hepatic presentations. The lesson teaches the qualitative rule only.

The reviewer states hepatitis A is self-limited and never chronic, which ACIP 2020 supports, but omits that 10–15% of symptomatic patients have prolonged or relapsing illness lasting up to 6 months, and that IgM anti-HAV can occasionally persist beyond a year or be falsely positive (so IgM is tested only in symptomatic suspected cases).

The 75–85% chronicity figure matches Chen and Morgan 2006, but CDC 2020 says only that more than half develop chronic infection and Uto 2012 gives 60–85%; estimates depend on cohort and age at infection.
